beats.headline: Stop writing manual Singletons.
beats.subline: Global state is a testing nightmare. Here is how modern Java handles shared instances.
beats.narration: Stop writing manual singletons. Global state is a testing nightmare. If you are using Spring, let the container manage your beans. If you are not, here is how to do it safely.

beats.title: Manual vs. Container Managed
beats.narration: Manual singletons hide dependencies and leak state between unit tests. Spring beans allow constructor injection, meaning every test gets a fresh, isolated instance.

beats.title: The Enum Singleton

steps.explanation: The JVM guarantees this is initialized exactly once, even with multithreading.
Java serialization and reflection explicitly block creating new enum instances.

beats.narration: For standalone tools, use an enum. The JVM guarantees thread-safe initialization, and it is immune to reflection hacks or deserialization bugs that plague traditional singleton patterns.

beats.title: Singleton Decision Tree
beats.narration: Always prefer DI containers first. If you are building a standalone library without a container, the Enum singleton is your safest, most robust choice.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): Factory Methods and Abstract Factories →
beats.narration: That covers singletons. In Part 2, we look at Factory Methods and Abstract Factories to decouple object creation from your business logic.

beats.headline: Stop hardcoding your dependencies.
beats.subline: Creating objects directly with 'new' locks you into concrete implementations.
beats.narration: Stop hardcoding dependencies. Using 'new' directly locks your service to a specific implementation. Factories let you swap behavior without touching your business logic.

beats.title: Factory Method Pattern

steps.explanation: Subclasses decide which concrete transport to instantiate.
The business logic remains agnostic of the specific transport implementation.

beats.narration: The Factory Method defines an abstract creation hook. Your business logic calls the hook, but subclasses decide if they want to send an email, SMS, or push notification.

beats.title: Abstract Factory: Families
beats.narration: Use Abstract Factory when you need a family of related objects. AWS S3 and EC2 belong together; mixing them with Azure blobs is a recipe for disaster.

beats.title: Factory vs. Supplier
beats.narration: Don't over-engineer. For simple cases, just pass a Supplier or a method reference. Only reach for Abstract Factory when you have a massive, related suite of objects.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
beats.narration: That is factories handled. In Part 3, we look at the Builder pattern and why Java records might make your custom builders obsolete.

beats.headline: Your Builder class is probably bloated.
beats.subline: If you are writing 50 lines of boilerplate for a simple config object, stop.
beats.narration: Your builder class is probably bloated. If you are writing 50 lines of boilerplate for a simple configuration object, you are doing it wrong. Let's look at the modern alternative.

beats.title: Builder vs. Record
beats.narration: If your object has only a few fields, a Java record is all you need. It gives you immutability and validation out of the box without the builder overhead.

beats.title: Fluent Step Builder

steps.explanation: Forces the user to provide mandatory fields in the correct order.
The builder won't even compile if a mandatory step is skipped.

beats.narration: When you have complex, mandatory steps, use a Step Builder. By returning interfaces, you force the caller to provide data in the exact order you define.

beats.title: When to use what?
beats.narration: Keep it simple. Records for data, Builders for complex optional configurations, and Step Builders only when you need to enforce a specific construction flow.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 4): Prototype and Final Summary →
beats.narration: Builders are powerful but often misused. In Part 4, we wrap up with the Prototype pattern and a final summary of when to use which pattern.

beats.headline: Cloneable is a design mistake.
beats.subline: Avoid the built-in clone() method. Here is the modern way to duplicate objects.
beats.narration: The built-in Cloneable interface is a historical mistake. It is fragile and unsafe. Here is how to handle object duplication in modern Java.

beats.title: Modern Copying

steps.explanation: List.copyOf ensures your internal state remains immutable.
Returns a new instance with a modified field—cleaner than cloning.

beats.narration: Use copy constructors or record 'with' methods. They are explicit, type-safe, and handle deep copies of mutable collections much better than the legacy clone method ever could.

beats.title: Creational Cheat Sheet
beats.narration: Stick to this roadmap. Use DI or Enums for singletons, Suppliers for factories, and Records or Builders for object construction. Keep it simple and readable.
